newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's race divide proves hard to bridge.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's race divide proves hard to bridge.

text.p: Three years after South Africa's transition to democracy, the uneven distribution of wealth and power threatens again to divide blacks and whites.
The euphoria of the country's first all-race elections in April 1994 promised to erase the racial divide that defined South African society for more than three centuries.
But two months ago President Nelson Mandela warned his parliament: "Today, in some ways, the old fault lines of our society are showing more sharply."

The new government promised jobs for all, a million new houses in the first five years of democracy and a better life for the five-to-one black majority relegated under white rule to soulless township ghettos.
But last month Mining Minister Penuel Maduna said blacks were getting tired of waiting for the fruits of democracy.
"There may arise a moment when we can't restrain them any longer and then we may turn into real tyrants and set dogs and police and soldiers on them when they say: 'We are hungry'."

Archbishop Desmond Tutu's statutory Truth Commission promised to be the public confessional in which the torturers, killers and social engineers of apartheid would find absolution for the human rights abuses that were their stock in trade.

But last month former president F.W. de Klerk, who repudiated apartheid in 1990 and handed power to Mandela four years later, accused Tutu of bias against his white-led National Party and sought redress in the High Court.

De Klerk warned parliament that the common purpose forged in the run-up to the first all-race election was splintering as Afrikaners found themselves more and more the target of the Truth Commission's probe into the history of white rule.
"The spirit of reconciliation has dimmed...We must find a way to handle the conflict of the past that does not encourage polarisation," he said.
Mandela's deputy and heir-apparent, Thabo Mbeki, put the crumbling post-apartheid consensus back on the public agenda last week (June 10) in his annual policy speech to parliament.

"This is a society which continues to be characterised by deep fissures which separate the black people from the white, the hungry from the prosperous, the urban from the rural, the male from the female, the disabled from the rest.

"Running like a structural fault through it all and weaving it together into a frightening bundle of imbalance and inequality is the question of race and colour -- the fundamental consideration on which South African society was built for 300 years," he said.
Urging the masters of apartheid to acknowledge their responsibility for the damage done by white rule, he said:
"The great crevices in our society...are also represented by the controversy which seems to have arisen around the work of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
"The hatreds and animosities of the past will not go away unless the truth is told about what happened."

Mandela has captured the imagination of the world with his lack of bitterness about the 27 years he spent in jail for opposing white rule, but at home patience is wearing thin over his failure to deliver visibly on the election promises of his African National Congress.
The Housing Department said in May it had passed the halfway mark on its promise of a million new houses during the term of the first black-led government.
But critics argue it has provided subsidies adequate only to finance a very basic single-roomed dwelling and has not physically built more than a handful of houses.

Whites continue to dominate the management echelons of the public service, the defence force and the police, unemployment remains higher at around 30 percent among blacks than it is among whites, and the reality of schooling remains bleaker for black children than for most of their white counterparts.

Crime has burst from the townships where it raged almost unchecked under apartheid into the still largely white suburbs. Corruption, ranging from the abuse of personal privileges to allegations of massive tender fraud, appears to be spreading.

Economic growth, projected in last year's Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy at 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997, looks set to fall below even Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's revised target of 2.5 percent.
Economists said last week that with growth slowing, there was little hope of achieving the Gear target of 400,000 new jobs a year by the turn of the century.
Mbeki, already in charge of the day-to-day running of South Africa, said last week the only way forward was to renew the search for a national consensus on a shared future.
"It is important that we resist the temptation to abandon this path and retreat into a laager, as some recent developments seem to suggest," he said.

"Collectively and individually, we have a responsibility to contribute to the making of the new democratic, non-racial, non-sexist, united and prosperous South Africa in the common interest of all the constituencies we represent."
